title: Wooden Blocks
strapline: Stack, topple, build again — small hands testing big ideas about balance and space.
intent: Explore balance, stability and gravity first-hand — how wide bases hold tall towers and why the wobbly one always falls
Feed enclosure and trajectory schemas: pens for the animals, walls around a world, ramps that send cars flying
Discover block mathematics — that two short blocks make one long one, and that an arch needs two matching pillars
Grow spatial and comparative language: on top, underneath, next to, longer, heavier, taller
Learn that a collapse is information, not failure — adjust, rebuild, keep going
Build together: sharing a structure means sharing a plan
implementation: Store blocks on shadow shelves sorted by shape, so every tidy-up is a matching game and children can see what is on offer
Sit low and build alongside children, sometimes quietly mirroring their structure to spark talk about matching and symmetry
Resist rebuilding a fallen tower for them — wonder aloud instead: "which block do you think made it wobble?"
Model precise spatial language as you play: "you've balanced the arch on top of two cylinders"
Add small-world animals and people nearby to provoke enclosures, homes and bridges
Offer planks and guttering with cars and balls so ramps and rolling become part of block play
Photograph impressive builds before tidy-up time and revisit the photos together to plan the next one
key_questions: How tall do you think it can go before it wobbles?
What could you use to make this side match that side?
Which blocks will roll down your ramp, and which will slide?
How will the animals get in and out of your pen?
What happened when you put the big one on top? What could you try instead?

impact.text: Our youngest builders fill, empty, stack and gleefully knock down — and go straight back for more.
Children hunt for the right block for a gap, turning and testing it until it fits the space.
Builds become deliberate — a bridge for the cars, a bed for the lion — and children tell you all about them as they work.
Children compare and describe their structures: "mine's longer", "that one's heavier", "put it next to the arch".
Children count blocks out for a build with one-to-one correspondence and know the last number tells them how many.
Symmetry and pattern appear: children mirror one side of a build on the other, or repeat a block sequence along a wall.
When a tower crashes, children have another go — wider base, steadier hands — rather than walking away.
Older children build with a plan — "I'm making a castle" — adapt when the arch keeps slipping, and negotiate shared builds with friends.

enhancements: Small-world farm animals and fence pieces beside the blocks to spark enclosures
Guttering, planks and a basket of cars and balls for ramp-and-roll testing
Photographs of local bridges and buildings — including ones the children pass every day — to build from
A mirror panel behind the block area so builds double themselves and symmetry talk starts naturally
Tape measures, clipboards and pencils for measuring and recording tower heights
Fabric squares and pegs so a build can grow a roof and become somewhere to be
A "please leave standing" sign children can write and place on a build they want to finish tomorrow

playing_exploring: Children return to the same tower problem day after day, trying their own ways in
Blocks have no instructions — every build starts from the child's own idea
active_learning: A collapse becomes information, not failure — children adjust the base, the block choice, the height, and try again
creating_thinking: Children form and test their own theories about balance — wide bottoms, flat tops, heavy blocks low down — and tell you what they have discovered
